And you need to dispose of the former completely. The portion of your
argument that declares MI to be "too powerful" is simply ludicrous, at
best. A single Wake suffices to block any number of Mirror Images, with
absolutely no cost to the Woken vampire -- because Mirror Image ends
combat, which does no damage to the blocker, who should then feel free
to repeatedly block until the actor runs out of Mirror Image.

The sole benefit to Mirror Image not being an action modifier is the
ability to play Mirror Image twice in two successive combats, and
potentially continuing the action beyond that. This only affects decks
which rely on leaving vampires untapped to block and do not pack Wakes
or other untap-like effects; such decks are already vulnerable to a
number of other, more powerful effects like Anarch Troublemaker.
Conceivably one could cycle Mirror Images out of one's hand until one
got hold of a Fata Morgana, Daring the Dawn, or other card to make the
action finally succeed -- the potential benefit to this is negligible,
especially considering the card costs a blood.

Thus, the initial portion of your argument is refuted. Please discard
it in future replies, as you simply don't have a leg to stand on here.

Now, on to the second portion of your argument. This is a much sounder
base from which to form your opinion, but there are still a number of
visible flaws in your arguments.

First, Mirror Image and Form of Mist are not identical effects. Mirror
Image costs a blood and is restricted to non-bleeding actions; Form of
Mist is free, provides +1 stealth, and can be used on any action. If
you consider that the 'action modifier' status of Form of Mist is a
deliberate restriction, then the one-blood cost is a clear matchup for
an equivalent restriction -- especially considering the effect is not as
powerful as Form of Mist.

Second, Mirror Image does not change anything about the action. It is
still the same action, it continues at the same stealth/intercept values
as before, it does not provide any additional benefits after the action
is completed -- nothing has changed about the action. Form of Mist
provides an obvious change to the action itself: the +1 stealth.

Third, the "inconsistency" argument is obviated by my initial
counterargument; the fact that they are different effects provides
sufficient logical basis for them to be covered by different card
classes. Note that there are three separate, yet distinct differences
between the two effects.

Fourth, there are long-standing policies concerning errata which, summed
up, state "as little as necessary". If Mirror Image received errata,
then Shadow Body, Chameleon's Colors, and Flow within the Mountain (all
of which are combat-only cards) would also require similar errata, as
they also all produce "continue the action" effects. It is worth noting
that each of these cards also costs a blood, and two of these cards also
have the "non-bleeding" restriction, making them all better matches for
Mirror Image than Form of Mist.

For a card which isn't even overpowered to begin with (see point #1),
generating widespread errata is clearly a Bad Idea. If you can break
it, I suggest you do so and then post the deck; but I don't see any way
to break the card, due to the 1-blood cost and non-bleeding restriction.

Which tournaments is it dominating? It is worth noting that practically
every too powerful card becomes taken up by schools of decks.
Practically every 'broken' card in existence has been abused in quick
time. Temptation of Greater Power is the obvious one that wasn't, and
Betrayer - but Betrayer *couldn't* be, until Sabbat was released. So
what tournaments is Mirror Image dominating, or nearly so (the decks may
still need some tweaks)? (Proof by experience.)

Given that Mirror Image does not provide stealth (one handicap) and
costs blood (a second handicap) is its effect more powerful than Form of
Mist, which is free (without that handicap) and with additional stealth
(a benefit) but is limited to one per action (its single handicap)? Can
you provide compelling evidence that a blood cost and no stealth is
significantly weaker than an action modifier restriction? This would be
proof by theory.

Many broken cards require whole shifts of decks to cater to them - for
instance, Return to Innocence, pre-errata Thoughts Betrayed. Mirror
Image, in the first instance, is foiled by anti-Strike: Combat Ends. If
you play Immortal Grapple (a common facet of the combat game), you
cannot have Mirror Image played against you, for instance.
Additionally, Wake with Evening's Freshness and Forced Awakening foil
Mirror Image, without extra work. (And if you could put in extra
stealth, you may well have been better off playing it *before* you got
blocked, and skip the Mirror Image entirely.) These are common facets
of the game also, because you build all decks knowing that you could be
tapped by a Mind Numb, a Misdirection or an Anarch Troublemaker, and
knowing that if you can both take actions *and* react (for a bounce, for
a block, for a Delaying Tactics etc.) you can do much more than if you
leave yourself untapped. Then there's the fact that, feeding back into
anti-S:CE above, there are several forms of defence that will shatter a
Mirror Image also - Psyche! and Telepathic Tracking will both kick in
before the continue action effect, causing it to fizzle. So... so far,
we have multiple common defences against it, that are both useful and
multi-functional. That would be a good proof that decks would have to
completely restructure themselves to defend against it.

Then we try to consider the card in the context of other cards that end
up generating the same-ish effect, in other ways. (Proof by analogy.)
Mirror Image doesn't provide any stealth, so effectively it just taps a
blocker - assuming you manage to pull it off. That could be generated
by a Master Card such as Misdirection or Anarch Troublemaker. (Single
card, master phase, possible pool cost.) Similarly, block denial could
be achieved with Seduction. Now, at superior this isn't going to
*actually* tap the vampire, but it might as well do, for that action,
unless something like Fast Reaction is going to be pulled out of the
bag. (Possible, but unlikely.) Seduction is a single card, no blood
cost, but it does get the action modifier restriction. But it's also in
Dominate, a highly potent discipline. In context, Chimerstry is a
secondary-resource manipulator, whereas Dominate goes a lot more for
primary resources. Dominate is the more 'offensive' discipline (in
terms of offence, rather than terms of being considered nasty, horrible
and smelly - though it does that too, sometimes), both offensively
(bleed modifiers) and defensively (bleed bounce), along with a fair
chunk of secondary resource manipulation, whereas Chimerstry is almost
solely dedicated to secondary resources. In total, also, Dominate is
available to uber-lots of vampires, whereas Chimerstry is available to
only a few vampires. ELDB is telling me that CHI is only available on
13 vampires, whereas DOM is on 95. Considered in context, then, we can
allow for Mirror Image being more slightly powerful than Seduction.

So we move on, what else can we compare it with? Call of the Hungry
Dead isn't a bad one. At inferior, it's free. Mirror Image is one
blood. At superior, it's burn one blood, Mirror Image is one blood. In
most circumstances, that wouldn't make much difference BUT both the
Giovanni (not the only Necromancers but...) and the Ravnos do benefit
from Path of Bone and Path of Paradox, and the Path of Bone won't work
on Call of the Hungry Dead, but Paradox will on Mirror Image. And Path
of Paradox isn't bad for the Ravnos - especially since some of their
cards are rather expensive. And unlike the Giovanni, they stand a
reasonable chance at defending it, with their intercept and stealth
denial. So there's a minor plus there, which could work out to be a
rather reasonable plus, in context. Of course, block denial is slightly
different to action continue, but we're doing proof by analogy. And it
can work out similar, in that the action carries on without that vampire
blocking. And Call of the Hungry Dead is more powerful, in that it
stops you going into combat and no amount of Wake with Evening's
Freshness will let you block with that vampire when it's played. Not
going into combat is, these days, not a thing to be sniffed at - this
also occurs with Seduction, above - block avoidance = no combat = safer.
People are playing anti-S:CE (uh-oh) and pro-combat. Psyche! with
blurred guns and the like. I'd rather have Call in that instance.
Similar comparisons could be made with Elder Impersonation, which is in
a different discipline - oh, and that costs 1 blood all the time, no
cost reduction for Obfuscate. Chimerstry and Necromancy work kind of
well as comparisons, even post-Bloodlines (with lots of new
Necromancers) in that they're relatively toolboxy disciplines - but of
course, Necromancy teams up with Dominate, whereas Chimerstry gets

to argue, as you are trying here, that the action ends the moment that
the acting minion was blocked, Uncontrollable Rage would not be usable
in the block combat - which it is. [LSJ 19980102 - Robert Goudie poses

[LSJ 20010316]

"What happens when a vampire enters combat with another minion
via Bum's Rush modified by an Uncontrollable Rage, and the
opposing minion plays S:CE, and the acting vampire plays superior
Psyche! to start combat again?."

We get (further down the thread):

The resolution of the Bum's Rush action was combat.
That combat is over.

But before the action ends, players get the opportunity to play
other effects, like Cats Guidance, Freak Drive, Psyche!, Hidden
Lurker, etc.

So, after resolution, the action is still there. But the example is
successful resolution. How does this impact on blocks?

[LSJ 20021217]

There's still a question of when the "taint" is applied and, in
the case of Mask, to whom. That's whence the question. The taint
is applied to the minion who is the acting minion when the
action resolves (successfully, blocked, ended, or otherwise).

The block and ensuing combat is, therefore, part of the resolution of an
unsuccessful action - it's just a different type of resolution to a
successful action. But per [LSJ 20010316], resolution doesn't end the
action. So after blocking, the action is still there.

All it does is postpone the end of the action, without changing anything
about the details of the action. The acting minion is still tapped.
The blocking minions are still tapped, though if they've played a Wake,
that effect remains in play (unchanged). The stealth is the same. The
basic action itself is still the same, with the same target.

Freak Drive modifies the action by untapping the acting minion.

Hidden Lurker modifies the action by allowing a non-acting minion to
enter combat, and putting restrictions on that combat.

At whether or not something changes the action.

No problem. I like Ravnos, so it's fun talking about playing them.

> Also.... intercepting inherintly results
> in a fight. As my strongest combat is hands for 1 I would rather just sit
> back... Sense Dep key minons... block troubling rushes with little chumps

Blocking gets you combat, but stop and think a moment about just how much
S:CE you have. You may not want to get in front of minions that can
overcome that, but there are plenty who can't. Deck space considerations
are valid, but a little intercept is never a bad thing.

> It's amazing how much 3 weenie CHI vamps
> can bleed for with Gabrin untaped. My Prey NEEDS to block what ever Gabrin
> does so he lets in a bleed for 2... and again... and again.... I when I
> build decks I find that a deck can do only so much.

Then you've had good experiences with this deck. I think your description
is still a little on the rosey side, though.

> Fight/Stealth/Intercept - a deck can do 2 of those thing reliably or it can
> do 1 to the exclusion of both others and it never has to worry about not
> having the right cards in hand.

"Fight" might also be taken to mean "surviving combat". You've already
got, what, twelve cards slots that incidently give you S:CE. You have
unintentionally stumbled onto a card that works about three different
ways. You might as well use it.

There are other items you could add to that
> short list.. Vote/Bleed but these are a "payload" and need a "delevery
> system". I just didn't want to water down the strengths of the deck with
> cards that I wouldn't see often enough to count on seeing them when I needed
> them. I'd rather use other cards to increase my payload or bolster my
> already in place defences. I have some combat defence and a stealth/pseudo
> stealth delivery system and I felt why water that down with intercept?
> Anyway.. build the deck. It's fun, it plays well, cycles nicely, I hardly
> every handjam with it.

I play a similiar one. Mine hardly ever handjams, either, but I've also
got Elder Library, two Dreams, Visit from Capuchin, and eight Red
Herrings, so it damn well better not.
